== APPRAISAL INSTRUCTIONS (GEMINI_HANDOFF_BRIEF §3 Task D; RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2; APPRAISAL_FORM.md; CODEBOOK.md §8) ==
1. ACCESSIBILITY GATE:
   - If `Retrieval status` is `not_accessible` (or the paper text below says `[FULL TEXT NOT ACCESSIBLE]`), you MUST set `paper_read = "not accessible"`, `study_design_identified = "cannot_tell (full text not accessible)"`, `chosen_tool = "cannot_tell"`, `why_tool_chosen = "full text not accessible"`, `overall_rating = "cannot_tell"`, `domain_ratings = []`, all 7 `cross_tool_domains` fields to `"cannot_tell"`, `overall_narrative_summary = "Full text not accessible; no risk-of-bias appraisal performed."`, `where_found_summary = "not accessible"`, and `evidence_quotes = []`. NEVER guess study design or bias ratings from citation/title!

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Some concern / Can't tell: Cross-sectional design without longitudinal follow-up, but sample denominators are inconsistently reported without reconciliation across chapters (400 voters randomly drawn at 100 per locality [PDF p. 70], non-located households replaced [PDF p. 71], 360 households surveyed at a reported 86% response rate [PDF p. 71], N = 318 stated in Table 3.1 and Section 3.2.2 [PDF pp. 69, 74], and n = 317 analyzed in Tables 4.1-4.6 [PDF pp. 92-101]; similarly, FGD totals are reported as n = 91 in Table 3.1 [PDF p. 69] versus 71 across subgroups in Table 3.4 [PDF p. 78]).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern: In the accessible RQ1 multivariate logistic regression (Section 4.3.2, PDF pp. 99-100), binary committee satisfaction is regressed solely on seven participatory indicators with zero adjustment for household socioeconomic status, gender, education, primary water source, or scheme fixed effects—despite large cross-scheme differences in demographics and satisfaction (81.0% in Wandiege vs. 16.5% in Paga; Tables 4.1-4.3) that severely confound pooled household associations. RQ2 similarly relies on unadjusted Chi-square tests (Table 3.1, PDF p. 69) and logistic models in truncated Chapter 5 with no confounder control strategy specified in Methods (Section 3.2.2, PDF p. 75).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak / indirect operationalization (partially unassessable for Chapter 6): Chapter 1 descriptively outlines informal tenure characteristics (PDF p. 17), Kenya's Water Reform Act of 2002 and KIWASCO's Delegated Management Model in Obunga (Section 1.3.2, PDF pp. 33-34), and community-elected self-help/trustee structures across the four schemes (Sections 1.3.1-1.3.4, PDF pp. 32-38), while the Table of Contents lists Section 6.2.5 ('Extent of Institutional Formalization', truncated after PDF p. 101). However, the quantitative models do not measure legal or institutional governance rules directly, relying instead on self-reported household participation and willingness items (Table 4.4, PDF p. 97).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern: Exposure (community participation) and outcome variables are unvalidated single-item self-report binary survey items administered face-to-face after community entry facilitated by local chiefs and SANA staff (PDF pp. 72-75, 94-100), creating strong social desirability and courtesy bias. Crucially, RQ1 analyzes all n = 317 respondents on satisfaction with the committee managing their 'main source of water' even though ~19% of respondents primarily relied on non-scheme sources (wells, boreholes, springs, rivers, private vendors; Table 4.2, PDF p. 94), misclassifying exposure and outcome, and regresses satisfaction on contemporaneous attitudinal willingness items (WILLTOPAY, CONTRIBUTION, INTERVENE).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak: Service performance and 'clean potable water supply' outcomes are measured solely through subjective single-item perceptions and self-reported behaviors/health histories—satisfaction with committee management (Table 4.3), satisfaction with water smell, self-reported cleaning/covering of storage containers, self-reported diagnosis/clinic visits for waterborne disease, and perceived access (Section 3.2.2, PDF p. 75; TOC PDF pp. 9-10)—without microbiological or physicochemical water testing or independent utility operational logs.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Can't tell (some concern): No study protocol or pre-analysis plan is mentioned (typical for a 2015 dissertation), internal sample counts vary without explanation across tables (360 vs. 318 vs. 317 survey; 91 vs. 71 FGD), and PDF pages 102-215 (Section 4.4, Chapters 5-7, and Appendices including the 57-item survey questionnaire in Appendix C) were truncated in the provided source text, preventing verification of whether all planned items and analyses were completely reported.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern: The four studied schemes (Wandiege, Obunga, Asengo, Paga) were purposively selected from seven SANA schemes in collaboration with SANA's director and scheme management teams specifically to contrast two high-performing, one average, and one poorly performing scheme (Section 3.5, PDF pp. 83-85). Within settlements, households were drawn from the 2012 Kenya Independent Voter Register (potentially excluding unregistered informal-settlement residents), located with local chiefs and SANA staff, and restricted to interviewing the eldest household member during 8:00 a.m.-5:00 p.m. field hours (PDF pp. 70-72), yielding a 59%-84% female sample (Table 4.1, PDF p. 92), with replacement of unlocated households. FGD participants were purposively sampled and interviewed at community water offices (PDF pp. 75-76).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S1: Are there clear research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: Section 1.2 explicitly states three research objectives, three research questions (RQ1 on community participation and beneficiary satisfaction with water management committees; RQ2 on positive/negative contributions of participation to clean potable water supply; RQ3 on participation-related factors affecting scheme performance), and three directional hypotheses (H1-H3).
domain_ratings.where_found: Abstract (PDF p. 12, p. vii); Section 1.2 (PDF pp. 28-29, pp. 15-16); Table 3.1 (PDF p. 69, p. 56)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S2: Do the collected data allow to address the research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: Primary household survey data (RQ1-RQ2) and 12 stratified focus group discussions supplemented by observations, transect walks, and archival records (RQ3) across the four SANA water schemes directly target the three stated research questions.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.1: Is the qualitative approach appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: An inductive qualitative approach is well suited to RQ3, which seeks to uncover contextual, social, and institutional participation-related mechanisms aiding or impeding community water scheme performance in urban informal settlements.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.2: Are the qualitative data collection methods adequate to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Data collection combined 12 purposively sampled FGDs (3 per scheme: women's group, water consumer group, and management committee) conducted in Luo using a structured questioning route and audio-recorded, alongside transect walks, unannounced site visits, meeting observations, and photographs. Minor caveats include hosting FGDs at community water offices and discrepancies between Table 3.1 (n = 91) and Table 3.4 subgroup counts (sum = 71).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.3: Are the findings adequately derived from the data?
domain_ratings.justification: Section 3.3.3 documents a systematic seven-stage Constant Comparison Analysis: translating Luo audio recordings into English, segmenting transcripts into meaningful chunks, coding unique statements, re-listening to tapes to verify quotes/codes, grouping codes into facilitating versus impeding themes, cross-case analysis, data triangulation with observation/transect-walk notes, and member checking with FGD participants.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.4: Is the interpretation of results sufficiently substantiated by data?
domain_ratings.justification: Although the Abstract (PDF p. 13) and Table of Contents (PDF p. 7) list the facilitating and impeding themes for RQ3, Chapter 6 (pp. 114-137) is truncated in the provided PDF text (which ends at PDF p. 101 / p. 88), making it impossible to verify whether qualitative interpretations are adequately backed by verbatim FGD quotations and observational evidence.
domain_ratings.where_found: Abstract & TOC (PDF pp. 7, 13, pp. ii, viii); Chapter 6 truncated after PDF p. 101

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.5: Is there coherence between qualitative data sources, collection, analysis and interpretation?
domain_ratings.justification: Design-level coherence between RQ3, multi-stakeholder FGDs/observations, and seven-stage constant comparative analysis is clear in Chapter 3, but truncation of Chapter 6 and Chapter 7 after PDF p. 101 prevents direct verification of coherence through final empirical presentation and interpretation.
domain_ratings.where_found: Table 3.1 & Section 3.3 (PDF pp. 69, 75-81, pp. 56, 62-68); Chapters 6-7 truncated after PDF p. 101

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative non-randomized 3.1: Are the participants representative of the target population?
domain_ratings.justification: First, the four studied schemes were purposively selected with SANA leadership to represent contrasting performance levels (two high, one average, one poor; Section 3.5). Second, within settlements, sampling relied on the 2012 Voter Register (excluding unregistered informal-settlement residents; note also the author's inaccurate claim that voting/registration is legally mandatory in Kenya), used chiefs and SANA staff to locate houses, interviewed only the eldest household member during 8:00 a.m.-5:00 p.m. field hours (yielding 59%-84% female respondents; Table 4.1), replaced unlocated households, and reported inconsistent totals without non-respondent analysis.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative non-randomized 3.2: Are measurements appropriate regarding both the outcome and intervention (or exposure)?
domain_ratings.justification: Exposures and outcomes rely on unvalidated single-item binary self-reports collected face-to-face after SANA/chief-facilitated community entry, without objective water-quality testing. Critically, RQ1 analyzes all n = 317 households on satisfaction with 'the committee responsible for managing your main source of water' despite ~19% of respondents primarily using non-scheme sources (wells, springs, rivers, boreholes, private vendors; Table 4.2), misclassifying both exposure and outcome, and uses contemporaneous willingness items (WILLTOPAY, CONTRIBUTION, INTERVENE) as exposures.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative non-randomized 3.3: Are there complete outcome data?
domain_ratings.justification: Sample numbers are inconsistently reported across sections without an attrition/exclusion breakdown: 400 voters initially selected (100 per locality, PDF p. 70), replacements drawn for unlocated households (PDF p. 71), 360 surveyed at a stated 86% response rate (PDF p. 71), N = 318 reported in Table 3.1/Section 3.2.2 (PDF pp. 69, 74), and n = 317 analyzed in Chapter 4 tables (PDF pp. 92-101), while Chapter 5 tables are truncated.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative non-randomized 3.4: Are the confounders accounted for in the design and analysis?
domain_ratings.justification: The multivariate logistic regression for RQ1 (Section 4.3.2) includes only the seven participation indicators and zero demographic, socioeconomic, water-source, or scheme fixed-effect controls—even though Table 4.1, Table 4.2, and Table 4.3 document major cross-scheme differences in gender, education, income, primary water source, and satisfaction (81.0% in Wandiege vs. 16.5% in Paga). RQ2 likewise specifies bivariate Chi-square tests (Table 3.1) with no confounding strategy described in Section 3.2.2.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative non-randomized 3.5: During the study period, is the intervention administered (or exposure occurred) as intended?
domain_ratings.justification: Because this is a cross-sectional post-hoc survey of schemes started between 1989/2007 and 2005, longitudinal fidelity of participatory governance was not tracked quantitatively; moreover, ~19% of surveyed households in the RQ1 analytic sample did not use a community-managed scheme as their main water source (Table 4.2), Paga experienced near-total collapse of active labor/meeting participation (Table 4.4), and Chapters 5-6 are truncated after PDF p. 101.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 1.3, Table 1.1, Tables 4.2 & 4.4 (PDF pp. 32-38, 94, 97, pp. 19-25, 81, 84); Chapters 5-6 truncated after PDF p. 101

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.1: Is there an adequate rationale for using a mixed methods design to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Sections 3.1 and 3.4 explicitly justify the 'partially mixed concurrent equal status design' in terms of triangulation, complementarity, addressing qualitative generalizability limits, capturing both structure and social process, and explaining quantitative associations qualitatively.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.2: Are the different components of the study effectively integrated to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Table 3.1 silos RQ1-RQ2 as purely quantitative ('Not Applicable' for qualitative) and RQ3 as purely qualitative ('Not Applicable' for quantitative), whereas Section 3.1 states data integration occurred after strand-level analysis, Section 4.1 briefly cross-references FGD/observation insights, and the List of Tables shows survey tables (Tables 6.1-6.2) embedded in qualitative Chapter 6. Because Section 4.4 and Chapters 5-7 are truncated after PDF p. 101, the effectiveness of actual cross-strand integration cannot be verified.
domain_ratings.where_found: List of Tables (PDF p. 10, p. v), Section 3.1 & Table 3.1 (PDF pp. 68-69, pp. 55-56), Section 4.1 (PDF p. 91, p. 78); Chapters 5-7 truncated after PDF p. 101

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.3: Are the outputs of the integration of qualitative and quantitative components adequately interpreted?
domain_ratings.justification: Truncation of the source text after PDF p. 101 omits the discussion and synthesis sections (Section 4.4, Chapter 5, Chapter 6, and Chapter 7), preventing assessment of how integrated quantitative-qualitative outputs were interpreted.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3.1 (PDF p. 68, p. 55); Section 4.4 and Chapters 5-7 truncated after PDF p. 101

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.4: Are divergences and inconsistencies between quantitative and qualitative results adequately addressed?
domain_ratings.justification: Section 3.4 notes 'fear of data incompatibility' at the question-design stage, but because Section 4.4 and Chapters 5-7 are truncated after PDF p. 101, it is not possible to determine whether empirical divergences between household survey regressions and FGD/observational evidence were identified and reconciled.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 3.4 (PDF p. 83, p. 70); Section 4.4 and Chapters 5-7 truncated after PDF p. 101

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.5: Do the different components of the study adhere to the quality criteria of each tradition of the methods involved?
domain_ratings.justification: The quantitative non-randomized component fails core epidemiological quality criteria due to unadjusted confounding across heterogeneous schemes (3.4 = No), single-item subjective measurement and exposure/outcome misclassification of ~19% non-scheme water users (3.2 = No), non-representative daytime eldest-member sampling and purposive scheme selection (3.1 = No), and unexplained sample-size discrepancies across tables.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Ananga (2015) is a primary mixed-methods PhD dissertation ('partially mixed concurrent equal status design') examining community participation in four NGO-sponsored (SANA) urban informal-settlement water schemes in Kisumu, Kenya (Wandiege, Obunga, Asengo, and Paga), combining a cross-sectional household questionnaire survey (RQ1-RQ2) with 12 focus group discussions, observations, and transect walks (RQ3). Appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT 2018; Qualitative 1.1-1.5, Quantitative non-randomized 3.1-3.5, Mixed Methods 5.1-5.5), the study has notable strengths in clear research questions (S1-S2), a well-justified mixed-methods rationale (5.1), multi-stakeholder local-language FGD data collection paired with transect walks and observations (1.1-1.2), and a clearly documented seven-stage constant comparative coding and member-checking protocol (1.3). However, per MMAT guidance that overall methodological quality cannot exceed the weakest component, overall risk of bias reflects high methodological concern driven by the quantitative non-randomized component (5.5 = No): (1) the four schemes were purposively chosen with SANA leadership to span high, average, and poor performance, while daytime (8:00 a.m.-5:00 p.m.) interviewing of the eldest household member via SANA/chief-assisted locating yielded a 59%-84% female sample (3.1 = No); (2) exposures and outcomes rely on unvalidated single-item self-reports without physical/microbiological water testing, and RQ1 includes all n = 317 respondents on committee satisfaction despite ~19% primarily using non-scheme water sources (3.2 = No); (3) the RQ1 multivariate logit omits all socioeconomic, demographic, water-source, and scheme fixed-effect confounders despite extreme cross-scheme heterogeneity (e.g., 81.0% satisfaction in Wandiege vs. 16.5% in Paga; 3.4 = No); and (4) sample denominators vary without reconciliation across chapters (400 selected, 360 surveyed, 318 in Table 3.1, 317 in Chapter 4; 91 vs. 71 FGD participants). Finally, because the provided source text was truncated after PDF page 101 of 215 (omitting Section 4.4, Chapters 5-7, and Appendices), qualitative result substantiation (1.4-1.5) and empirical mixed-methods integration (5.2-5.4) are rated 'Can't tell'.
raw_response.overall_rating: High methodological concern (limited by weakest quantitative non-randomized component; qualitative substantiation and mixed-methods integration items rated Can't tell due to truncation after PDF p. 101; no numeric score per MMAT 2018)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Concurrent mixed-methods study ('partially mixed concurrent equal status design') combining an analytical cross-sectional household questionnaire survey (n = 317/318 analyzed from 360 surveyed) with qualitative focus group discussions (12 FGDs), observations, and transect walks across four community-managed urban water schemes
raw_response.where_found_summary: PDF pages 1-101 of 215 were accessible in the provided source text (PDF pages 102-215 truncated). Accessible sections cover Front Matter, Table of Contents, List of Tables/Figures, and Abstract (PDF pp. 1-13, pp. i-viii); Chapter 1 Introduction, RQs/Hypotheses, and descriptions of the four Kisumu water schemes (PDF pp. 14-42, pp. 1-29); Chapter 2 Literature Review (PDF pp. 43-64, pp. 30-51); complete Chapter 3 Methods covering mixed-methods design, survey sampling/analysis, FGDs/observations/constant comparative analysis, scheme selection, data quality, and IRB ethics (PDF pp. 65-89, pp. 52-76); and Chapter 4 RQ1 descriptive statistics and bivariate/multivariate logit models up to Table 4.5 header (PDF pp. 90-101, pp. 77-88). Section 4.4, Chapters 5-7, References, and Appendices A-J (PDF pp. 102-215) were truncated.
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: Chapter 3 (Section 3.1, PDF pp. 67-69) explicitly designs and executes a primary empirical mixed-methods study ('partially mixed concurrent equal status design') integrating a quantitative household survey strand (RQ1-RQ2, analyzed via logistic regression and Chi-square tests) with a qualitative strand of 12 focus group discussions, observations, and transect walks (RQ3, analyzed via Constant Comparison Analysis). Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, genuine mixed-methods primary studies combining qualitative and quantitative empirical components must be appraised with the MMAT (using Quantitative non-randomized items 3.1-3.5 for the analytical cross-sectional exposure-outcome survey component alongside Screening S1-S2, Qualitative 1.1-1.5, and Mixed-Methods 5.1-5.5).
